question: Six claims, each resting on a difference between two numbers. Which differences are real, and which could easily be luck?
answer: A difference means nothing without the count behind it. Sixty per cent of 50 tasters is close to a coin toss; sixty per cent of 10,000 tosses is a bent coin. Small counts swing wildly on their own, which is why the most dramatic headlines so often rest on the smallest numbers.
move: Before trusting a change, ask how big a change luck alone makes.
ask: Which result did I last celebrate that rested on a handful of cases?

items.verdict: A fair coin gives 30 or more heads out of 50 about one time in ten.
The same 60%. Over 10,000 tosses, luck alone would essentially never get there.

items.note: Cases near a phone mast doubled, from 2 to 4.
items.verdict: With counts this small, 2 one year and 4 the next is everyday wobble.

items.note: The national rate fell from 5.1% to 5.0%.
items.verdict: It comes from a survey that wobbles by more than that. A 0.1 point move is noise.

items.note: Deaths fell from 10% to 8% among 30,000 patients.
items.verdict: That is 1,500 deaths against 1,200. With numbers this big, 300 is no fluke.

items.note: A class of 30 passes 4 points more than last year.
items.verdict: One pupil is over 3 points of a class of 30. One extra pass explains it.

source: Binomial arithmetic; ONS Labour Force Survey
reference: Binomial distribution: P(X >= 30) for 50 fair tosses = 0.10; 6,000 of 10,000 is 20 standard deviations from 5,000; ONS, A guide to labour market statistics: sampling variability of the unemployment rate
